bookTitle: Technical Analysis of the Financial Markets (John J. Murphy)

facts.statement: A Principal-Protected Note (PPN) is a structured financial product created by combining a zero-coupon government bond paying face value at maturity with a call option (or portfolio of call options) on an underlying asset or stock index. This guarantees 100% principal preservation on the downside while providing upside market participation if the underlying asset appreciates.

facts.topic: Covered Call Strategy Formulas and Payoff
facts.statement: A covered call consists of a long stock position combined with a short call option on the same stock. Its downside break-even equals Stock Purchase Price minus Call Premium Received, and its maximum profit equals (Call Strike Price minus Stock Purchase Price) plus Call Premium Received.

sourceCitation.book: Technical Analysis of the Financial Markets (John J. Murphy)
sourceCitation.excerpt: Downside Break-Even = Stock Purchase Price - Call Premium Received ... Maximum Profit = (Call Strike Price - Stock Purchase Price) + Call Premium Received

formulaDetails.name: Covered Call Break-Even and Max Profit
formulaDetails.latex: \text{Downside Break-Even} = S_0 - c, \quad \text{Maximum Profit} = (K - S_0) + c

payoffVsProfit.explanation: The covered call caps upside profit at strike K while providing downside cushioning equal to the short call premium received c.

facts.statement: A protective put consists of a long stock position combined with a long put option on the same stock, providing capped maximum loss and uncapped upside potential. Its break-even price equals Stock Purchase Price plus Put Premium Paid, and its maximum loss equals (Stock Purchase Price minus Put Strike Price) plus Put Premium Paid.

sourceCitation.book: Technical Analysis of the Financial Markets (John J. Murphy)
sourceCitation.excerpt: Break-Even Price = Stock Purchase Price + Put Premium Paid ... Maximum Loss = (Stock Purchase Price - Put Strike Price) + Put Premium Paid

facts.topic: Bull Call Spread Formulas and Payoff
facts.statement: A bull call spread is established by buying a call with lower strike K_1 and selling a call with higher strike K_2 (K_1 < K_2) as a net debit transaction. Its break-even price equals K_1 plus Net Debit, and its maximum profit equals (K_2 minus K_1) minus Net Debit.

sourceCitation.excerpt: Break-Even Price = K_1 + Net Debit ... Maximum Profit = (K_2 - K_1) - Net Debit

facts.topic: Box Spread Arbitrage Present Value Rule
facts.statement: A box spread combines a bull call spread and a bear put spread using the same strikes K_1 < K_2, guaranteeing a terminal payoff of K_2 minus K_1 regardless of stock price S_T. In an arbitrage-free market, the initial net debit must equal the present value of (K_2 - K_1) discounted at the risk-free rate: Box Price = (K_2 - K_1) * e^(-r*T).

sourceCitation.book: Technical Analysis of the Financial Markets (John J. Murphy)

facts.statement: A butterfly spread consists of buying one call at lower strike K_1, buying one call at higher strike K_3, and selling two calls at middle strike K_2 (where K_2 = (K_1 + K_3) / 2) for a net debit. Its maximum profit equals (K_2 minus K_1) minus Net Debit, with downside break-even at K_1 plus Net Debit and upside break-even at K_3 minus Net Debit.

sourceCitation.book: Technical Analysis of the Financial Markets (John J. Murphy)
sourceCitation.excerpt: Downside Break-Even = K_1 + Net Debit; Upside Break-Even = K_3 - Net Debit ... Maximum Profit = (K_2 - K_1) - Net Debit

formulaDetails.name: Butterfly Spread Break-Even and Max Profit
formulaDetails.latex: \text{Max Profit} = (K_2 - K_1) - \text{Net Debit}, \quad \text{Downside BE} = K_1 + \text{Net Debit}, \quad \text{Upside BE} = K_3 - \text{Net Debit}

generalAssumptions: Principal-Protected Notes require a sufficient interest rate discount on zero-coupon government bonds to fund option premiums.
Spread and combination strategies are executed with standardized options sharing the same underlying asset and expiration date.
Box spreads and option combinations trade in efficient markets where mispricings below the discounted present value of terminal payoffs present riskless arbitrage opportunities.
